items.headline: LiveMACE: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agent Capabilities in Evolving Markets
items.summary: Evaluating agents by outcomes alone can obscure the capabilities that produce them. This problem is especially pronounced in evolving environments, where outcomes reflect a closed-loop interaction between agent behavior and changing external conditions. We introduce LiveMACEBench, a process-aware benchmark that uses live financial markets as a naturally evolving testbed for persistent LLM agents.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Five frontier LLMs operate along continuous trajectories under matched Tool Use, Persistent Memory, Rule Following, and Multi-Agent Collaboration configurations. We evaluate them through both realized outcomes and mechanism-specific diagnostics derived from complete decision traces. Across 30 days of live evaluation, we find a pronounced outcome-capability gap: realized returns often diverge from capability-specific measurements, and similar outcomes can arise from markedly different patterns of mechanism use. Trace-level diagnostics further expose distinct bottlenecks across capabilities, demonstrating that mechanism access, effective mechanism use, and downstream performance are not interchangeable measures of agent capability. LiveMACEBench makes this distinction measurable, turning live markets from a performance leaderboard into a diagnostic environment for agent capability

items.headline: Scene-Designer: Learning Design Intelligence for Agentic 3D Scene Generation
items.summary: Generating complete, coherent, and usable 3D indoor scenes from natural language requires strong design intelligence: the ability to design high-quality scenes and critique their quality. However, existing approaches either rely on general-purpose models lacking domain-specific design experience or learn from static scenes. In this work, we introduce Scene-Designer, an agentic framework that learns design intelligence through complementary design and critique experiences.

Based on these experiences, we propose Scene-GRPO, a Critic-guided GRPO framework that improves design decisions and reduces unnecessary trial-and-error corrections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Scene-Designer achieves superior performance in physical validity, functional correctness, and layout coherence, while the learned Scene-Critic significantly outperforms general-purpose models in scene critique. Moreover, test-time Critic guidance further improves scene generation, showing that the Critic can provide useful guidance beyond training. Additional analysis suggests a trend of mutual enhancement between scene design and critique abilities.

items.headline: BridgeWAM: Bridging Video and Action Experts via Latent Bridge Queries
items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.

items.headline: Learning to Think and Explore in 3D World. We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space.
items.summary: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.

items.headline: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics
items.summary: The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics: the embedding and the unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods either reuse a fixed lens or treat the states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state the way the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adaptive to the context.

We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adaptive to the context.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Lexical reference frames approximate it by reading a state through the model's own remaining layers with a stated number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, without fitting to the model's output. No lens, with fixed directions per layer, can exceed the square root of the native frame's coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, whereas the first-order frame, LexFrame[1], reaches 0.97 and 0.97 and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model's output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, its lexical basis steers a prediction while sparing other tokens, and its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, where lenses skip almost none. In this way, lexical reference frames make every hidden state of the model readable, attributable and steerable.

items.headline: RAP: A Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars
items.summary: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.

items.headline: Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text.
items.summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text. Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering.

detail.method_architecture: Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we observe direct but uneven transfer from visual supervision to language. Motivated by these observations, we successively introduce Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image--Text Alignment, which connect generation and answering through shared knowledge and interleaved responses, respectively. Guidance on selected entities can improve knowledge access on other entities without QA supervision, with additional gains from interleaved alignment. Further analysis shows that knowledge correctly reproduced in images is often more accessible through text, although substantial gaps remain between the two forms of access. These findings support visual generation as a source of knowledge beyond textual supervision, and motivate joint investigation of training data design and model architecture to make this knowledge more broadly accessible.

items.headline: Doom GPU Flame Graphs
items.summary: Imagine halving the resource costs of AI and what that could mean for the planet and the industry -- based on extreme estimates such savings could reduce the total US power usage by over 10% by 2030 1 . At Intel we've been creating a new analyzer tool to help reduce AI costs called AI Flame Graphs : a visualization that shows an AI accelerator or GPU hardware profile along with the full software stack, based on my CPU flame graphs . Our first version is available to customers in the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (previously called Ponte Vecchio).

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Here is an example: Simple example: SYCL matrix multiply microbenchmark (Click for interactive SVG .) The green frames are the actual instructions running on the AI or GPU accelerator, aqua shows the source code for these functions, and red (C), yellow (C++), and orange (kernel) show the CPU code paths that initiated these AI/GPU programs. The gray "-" frames just help highlight the boundary between CPU and AI/GPU code. The x-axis is proportional to cost, so you look for the widest things and find ways to reduce them. Layers This flame graph shows a simple program for SYCL (a high-level C++ language for accelerators) that tests three implementations of matrix multiply, running them with the same input workload. The flame graph is dominated by the slowest implementation, multiply_basic(), which doesn't use any optimizations and consumes at 72% of stall samples and is shown as the widest tower. On the right are two thin towers for multiply_local_access() at 21% which replaces the accessor with a local variable, and multiply_local_access_and_tiling() at 6% which also adds matrix tiling. The towers are getting smaller as optimizations are added. This flame graph profiler is a prototype based on Intel EU stall profiling for hardware profiling and eBPF for software instrumentation. It's designed to be easy and low-overhead , just like a CPU profiler. You should be able to generate a flame graph of an existing AI workload whenever you want, without having to restart anything or launch additional code via an interposer. Instruction-offset Profiling This is not the first project to build an AI profiler or even something called an AI Flame Graph, however, others I've seen focus on tracing CPU stacks and timing accelerator execution, but don't profile the instruction offsets running on the accelerator; or do profile them but via expensive binary instrumentation. I wanted to build AI flame graphs that work like CPU flame graphs: Easy to use, negligible cost, production safe, and shows everything. A daily tool for developers, with most of the visualization in the language of the developer : source code functions. This has been an internal AI project at Intel for the past year. Intel was already investing in this space, building the EU stall profiler capability for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series that provides an approximation of HW instruction sampling. I was lucky to have Dr. Matthew (Ben) Olson , an Intel AI engineer who has also worked on eBPF performance tooling ( processwatch ) as well as memory management research, join my team and do most of the development work. His background has helped us power through difficulties that seemed insurmountable. We've also recently been joined by Dr. Brandon Kammerdiener (coincidentally another graduate of the University of Tennessee, like Ben), who also has eBPF and memory internals experience, and has been helping us take on harder and harder workloads. And Gabriel Muñoz just joined today to help with releases. Now that our small team has shown that this is possible, we'll be joined by other teams at Intel to develop this further. We could have built a harder-to-use and higher-overhead version months ago using Intel GTPin but for widespread adoption it needs minimal overhead and ease of use so that developers don't hesitate to use this daily and to add it to deployment pipelines. What's a Flame Graph? A flame graph is a visualization I invented in 2011 for showing sampled code stack traces. It has become the standard for CPU profiling and analysis, helping developers quickly find performance improvements and eliminate regressions. A CPU flame graph shows the "big picture" of running software, with x-axis proportional to CPU cost. The example picture on the right summarizes how easy it can be to go from compute costs to responsible code paths. Prior to flame graphs, it could take hours to understand a complex profile by reading through hundreds of pages of output . Now it takes seconds: all you have to do is look for the widest rectangles. Flame graphs have had worldwide adoption. They have been the basis for five startups so far, have been adopted in over thirty performance analysis products, and have had over eighty implementations . My first implementation of flame graphs took a few hours on a Wednesday night after work. The real effort has been in the decade since, where I worked with different profilers, runtimes, libraries, kernels, compilers, and hypervisors to get flame graphs working properly in different environments, including fixing stack walking and symbolization. Earlier this year I posted about the final missing piece: Helping distros enable frame pointers so that profiling works across standard system libraries. Similar work is necessary for AI workloads: fixing stacks and symbols and getting profiling to work for different hardware, kernel drivers, user-mode drivers, frameworks, runtimes, languages, and models. A lot more work, too, as AI analysis has less maturity than CPU analysis. Searching Samples If you are new to flame graphs, it's worth mentioning the built-in search capability. In the earlier example, most of the stall samples are caused by sbid: software scoreboard dependency. As that may be a unique search term, you can run search (Ctrl-F, or click "Search") on "sbid" and it will highlight it in magenta: Search also shows the total number of stack samples that contained sbid in the bottom right: 78.4%. You can search for any term in the flame graph: accelerator instructions, source paths, function names, etc., to quickly calculate the percentage of stacks where it is present (excluding vertical overlap) helping you prioritise performance work. Note that the samples are EU stall-based, which means theoretical performance wins can take the percentages down to zero. This is different to timer-based samples as are typically used in CPU profiling. Stalls mean you better focus on the pain, the parts of the code that aren't making forward progress, but you aren't seeing resource usage by unstalled instructions. I'd like to supuport timer-based samples in the future as well, so we can have both views. Who will use this? At a recent golang conference, I asked the audience of 200+ to raise their hands if they were using CPU flame graphs. Almost every hand went up. I know of companies where flame graphs are a daily tool that developers use to understand and tune their code, reducing compute costs. This will become a daily tool for AI developers. My employer will use this as well for evaluation analysis, to find areas to tune to beat competitors, as well as to better understand workload performance to aid design. Why is AI profiling hard? Consider CPU instruction profiling: This is easy when the program and symbol table are both in the file system and in a standardized file format (such as ELF) as is the case with native compiled code (C). CPU profiling gets hard for JIT-complied code, like Java, as instructions and symbols are dynamically generated and placed in main memory (the process heap) without following a universal standard. For such JITted code we use runtime-specific methods and agents to retrieve snapshots of the heap information, which is different for each runtime. AI workloads also have different runtimes (and frameworks, languages, user-mode drivers, compilers, etc.) any of which can require special tinkering to get their CPU stacks and symbols to work. These CPU stacks are shown as the red, orange, and yellow frames in the AI Flame Graph. Some AI workloads are easy to get these frames working, some (like PyTorch) are a lot more work. But the real challenge is instruction profiling of actual GPU and AI accelerator programs -- shown as the aqua and green frames -- and correctly associating them with the CPU stacks beneath them. Not only may these GPU and AI programs not exist in the file system, but they may not even exist in main memory! Even for running programs. Once execution begins, they may be deallocated from main memory and only exist in special accelerator memory, beyond the direct reach of OS profilers and debuggers. Or within reach, but only through a prohibitively high-overhead HW-specific debugger interface. There's also no /proc representation for these programs either (I've been proposing building an equivalent) so there's no direct way to even tell what is running and what isn't, and all the other /proc details. Forget instruction profiling, even ps(1) and all the other process tools do not work. It's been a mind-bending experience, revealing what gets taken for granted because it has existed in CPU land for decades: A process table. Process tools. Standard file formats. Programs that exist in the file system. Programs running from main memory. Debuggers. Profiliers. Core dumping. Disassembling. Single stepping. Static and dynamic instrumentation. Etc. For GPUs and AI, this is all far less mature. It can make the work exciting at times, when you think something is impossible and then find or devise a way. Fortunately we have a head start as some things do exist. Depending on the runtime and kernel driver, there are debug interfaces where you can list running accelerator programs and other statistics, as used by tools like intel_gpu_top(1). You can kill -9 a GPU workload using intel_gpu_abrt(1). Some interfaces can even generate basic ELF files for the running accelerator programs that you can try to load in a debugger like gdb(1). And there is support for GPU/AI program disassembly, if you can get your hands on the binary. It feels to me like GPU/AI debugging, OS style, is about two years old. Better than zero, but still early on, and lots more ahead of us. A decade, at least. What do AI developers think of this? We've shown AI Flame Graphs to other AI developers at Intel and a common reaction is to be a bit puzzled, wondering what to do with it. AI developers think about their bit of code, but with AI Flame Graphs they can now see the entire stack for the first time, including the HW, and many layers they don't usually think about or don't know about. It basically looks like a pile of gibberish with their code only a small part of the flame graph. CPU Flame Graph Implementations This reaction is similar to people's first experiences with CPU flame graphs, which show parts of the system that developers and engineers typically don't work on, such as runtime internals, system libraries, and kernel internals. Flame graphs are great at highlighting the dozen or so functions that matter the most, so it becomes a problem of learning what those functions do across a few different code bases, which are typically open source. Understanding a dozen such functions can take a few hours or even a few days -- but if this leads to a 10% or 2x cost win, it is time well spent. And the next time the user looks at a flame graph, they start saying "I've seen that function before" and so on. You can get to the point where understanding the bulk of a CPU flame graph takes less than a minute: look for the widest tower, click to zoom, read the frames, done. I'm encouraged by the success of CPU flame graphs, with over 80 implementations and countless real world case studies. Sometimes I'm browsing a performance issue I care about on github and hit page down and there's a CPU flame graph. They are everywhere. I expect AI developers will also be able to understand AI Flame Graphs in less than a minute, but to start with people will be spending a day or more browsing code bases they didn't know were involved. Publishing case studies of found wins will also help people learn how to interpret them, and also help explain the value. What about PyTorch? Another common reaction we've had is that AI developers are using PyTorch, and initially we didn't support it as it meant walking Python stacks, which isn't trivial. But prior work has been done there (to support CPU profiling) and after a lot of tinkering we now have the first PyTorch AI Flame Graph: PyTorch frames in pink (Click for interactive SVG .) The PyTorch functions are at the bottom and are colored pink. This example runs oneDNN kernels that are JIT-generated, and don't have a source path so that layer just reads "jit". Getting all other the layers included was a real pain to get going, but an important milestone. We think if we can do PyTorch we can do anything. In this flame graph, we show PyTorch running the Llama 2 7B model using the Intel Extensions for PyTorch (IPEX). This flame graph shows the origin of the GPU kernel execution all the way back to the Python source code shown in pink. Most samples are from a stack leading up to a gemm_kernel (matrix multiply) shown in aqua, which like the previous example has many stalls due to software scoreboarding. There are two instructions (0xa30 and 0xa90) that combined are 27% of the entire profile. I expect someone will ask: Can't we just click on instructions and have it bring up a dissassembly view with full source? Yes, that should be possible, but I can't answer how we're going to provide this yet. Another expected question I can't yet answer: Since there are now multiple products providing AI auto-tuning of CPU workloads using CPU flame graphs (including Intel Granulate ) can't we have AI auto-tuning of AI workloads using AI Flame Graphs? First Release: Sometimes hard and with moderate overhead Getting AI Flame Graphs to work with some workloads is easy, but others are currently hard and cost moderate overhead. It's similar to CPU profiling, where some workloads and languages are easy to profile, whereas others need various things fixed. Some AI workloads use many software dependencies that need various tweaks and recompilation (e.g., enabling frame pointers so that stack walking works) making setup time consuming. PyTorch is especially difficult and can take over a week of OS work to be ready for AI Flame Graphs. We will work on getting these tweaks changed upstream in their respective repositories, something involving teams inside and outside of Intel, and is a process I'd expect to take at least a year. During that time AI workloads will gradually become easier to flame graph, and with lower-overhead as well. I'm reminded of eBPF in the early days: You had to patch and recompile the kernel and LLVM and Clang, which could take multiple days if you hit errors. Since then all the eBPF dependency patches have been merged, and default settings changed, so that eBPF "just works." We'll get there with AI Flame Graphs too, but right now it's still those early days. The changes necessary for AI Flame Graphs are really about improving debugging in general, and are a requirement for Fast by Friday : A vision where we can root-cause analyze anything in five days or less. Availability AI Flame Graphs will first become available on the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview feature for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series. If you are currently deployed there you can ask through the Intel service channel for early access. As for if or when it will support other hardware types, be in other Intel products, be officially launched, be open source, etc., these involve various other teams at Intel and they need to make their own announcements before I can discuss them here. Conclusions Finding performance improvements for AI data centers of just fractions of a percent can add up to planetary savings in electricity, water, and money. If AI flame graphs have the success that CPU flame graphs have had, I'd expect finding improvements of over 10% will be common, and 50% and higher will eventually be found*. But it won't be easy in these early days as there are still many software components to tweak and recompile, and software layers to learn about that are revealed in the AI flame graph. In the years ahead I imagine others will build their own AI flame graphs that look the same as this one, and there may even be startups selling them, but if they use more difficult-to-use and higher-overhead technologies I fear they could turn companies off the idea of AI flame graphs altogether and prevent them from finding sorely needed wins. This is too important to do badly. AI flame graphs should be easy to use, cost negligible overhead, be production safe, and show everything. Intel has proven it's possible. Disclaimer * This is a personal blog post that makes personal predictions but not guarantees of possible performance improvements. Feel free to take any claim with a grain of salt, and feel free to wait for an official publication and public launch by Intel on this technology. 1 Based on halving the Arm CEO Rene Haas' estimate of 20-25% quoted in Taking a closer look at AI's supposed energy apocalypse by Kyle Orland of ArsTechnica. Updates (Jan 2025): I wasn't going to talk about other specific profilers, but since FAQ #1 is "what about NVIDIA?": They do have flame graphs in Nsight Graphics for GPU workloads, so I'd guess they aren't far from supporting AI workloads as well. Their version looks shallow as it's only the GPU code, so it is missing the CPU context necessary to understand the full picture, and seems based on interposing (launching the app from Nsights) which is the old method. The new method we've created allows for easy, everything, anytime profiling, like you expect from CPU profilers. Theirs does have click-to-source integration, which is quite handy, and I do like the default orientation and colors, thank you! Thanks Thanks to everyone at Intel who have helped us make this happen. Markus Flierl has driven this project and made it a top priority, and Greg Lavender has expressed his support. Special thanks to Michael Cole, Matthew Roper, Luis Strano, Rodrigo Vivi, Joonas Lahtinen, Stanley Gambarin, Timothy Bauer, Brandon Yates, Maria Kraynyuk, Denis Samoylov, Krzysztof Raszkowski, Sanchit Jain, Po-Yu Chen, Felix Degrood, Piotr Rozenfeld, Andi Kleen, and all of the other coworkers that helped clear things up for us, and thanks in advance for everyone else who will be helping us in the months ahead. My final thanks is to the companies and developers who do the actual hands-on work with flame graphs, collecting them, examining them, finding performance wins, and applying them. You are helping save the planet.

We've shown AI Flame Graphs to other AI developers at Intel and a common reaction is to be a bit puzzled, wondering what to do with it. AI developers think about their bit of code, but with AI Flame Graphs they can now see the entire stack for the first time, including the HW, and many layers they don't usually think about or don't know about. It basically looks like a pile of gibberish with their code only a small part of the flame graph. CPU Flame Graph Implementations This reaction is similar to people's first experiences with CPU flame graphs, which show parts of the system that developers and engineers typically don't work on, such as runtime internals, system libraries, and kernel internals. Flame graphs are great at highlighting the dozen or so functions that matter the most, so it becomes a problem of learning what those functions do across a few different code bases, which are typically open source. Understanding a dozen such functions can take a few hours or even a few days -- but if this leads to a 10% or 2x cost win, it is time well spent. And the next time the user looks at a flame graph, they start saying "I've seen that function before" and so on. You can get to the point where understanding the bulk of a CPU flame graph takes less than a minute: look for the widest tower, click to zoom, read the frames, done. I'm encouraged by the success of CPU flame graphs, with over 80 implementations and countless real world case studies. Sometimes I'm browsing a performance issue I care about on github and hit page down and there's a CPU flame graph. They are everywhere. I expect AI developers will also be able to understand AI Flame Graphs in less than a minute, but to start with people will be spending a day or more browsing code bases they didn't know were involved. Publishing case studies of found wins will also help people learn how to interpret them, and also help explain the value. What about PyTorch? Another common reaction we've had is that AI developers are using PyTorch, and initially we didn't support it as it meant walking Python stacks, which isn't trivial. But prior work has been done there (to support CPU profiling) and after a lot of tinkering we now have the first PyTorch AI Flame Graph: PyTorch frames in pink (Click for interactive SVG .) The PyTorch functions are at the bottom and are colored pink. This example runs oneDNN kernels that are JIT-generated, and don't have a source path so that layer just reads "jit". Getting all other the layers included was a real pain to get going, but an important milestone. We think if we can do PyTorch we can do anything. In this flame graph, we show PyTorch running the Llama 2 7B model using the Intel Extensions for PyTorch (IPEX). This flame graph shows the origin of the GPU kernel execution all the way back to the Python source code shown in pink. Most samples are from a stack leading up to a gemm_kernel (matrix multiply) shown in aqua, which like the previous example has many stalls due to software scoreboarding. There are two instructions (0xa30 and 0xa90) that combined are 27% of the entire profile. I expect someone will ask: Can't we just click on instructions and have it bring up a dissassembly view with full source? Yes, that should be possible, but I can't answer how we're going to provide this yet. Another expected question I can't yet answer: Since there are now multiple products providing AI auto-tuning of CPU workloads using CPU flame graphs (including Intel Granulate ) can't we have AI auto-tuning of AI workloads using AI Flame Graphs? First Release: Sometimes hard and with moderate overhead Getting AI Flame Graphs to work with some workloads is easy, but others are currently hard and cost moderate overhead. It's similar to CPU profiling, where some workloads and languages are easy to profile, whereas others need various things fixed. Some AI workloads use many software dependencies that need various tweaks and recompilation (e.g., enabling frame pointers so that stack walking works) making setup time consuming. PyTorch is especially difficult and can take over a week of OS work to be ready for AI Flame Graphs. We will work on getting these tweaks changed upstream in their respective repositories, something involving teams inside and outside of Intel, and is a process I'd expect to take at least a year. During that time AI workloads will gradually become easier to flame graph, and with lower-overhead as well. I'm reminded of eBPF in the early days: You had to patch and recompile the kernel and LLVM and Clang, which could take multiple days if you hit errors. Since then all the eBPF dependency patches have been merged, and default settings changed, so that eBPF "just works." We'll get there with AI Flame Graphs too, but right now it's still those early days. The changes necessary for AI Flame Graphs are really about improving debugging in general, and are a requirement for Fast by Friday : A vision where we can root-cause analyze anything in five days or less. Availability AI Flame Graphs will first become available on the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview feature for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series. If you are currently deployed there you can ask through the Intel service channel for early access. As for if or when it will support other hardware types, be in other Intel products, be officially launched, be open source, etc., these involve various other teams at Intel and they need to make their own announcements before I can discuss them here. Conclusions Finding performance improvements for AI data centers of just fractions of a percent can add up to planetary savings in electricity, water, and money. If AI flame graphs have the success that CPU flame graphs have had, I'd expect finding improvements of over 10% will be common, and 50% and higher will eventually be found*. But it won't be easy in these early days as there are still many software components to tweak and recompile, and software layers to learn about that are revealed in the AI flame graph. In the years ahead I imagine others will build their own AI flame graphs that look the same as this one, and there may even be startups selling them, but if they use more difficult-to-use and higher-overhead technologies I fear they could turn companies off the idea of AI flame graphs altogether and prevent them from finding sorely needed wins. This is too important to do badly. AI flame graphs should be easy to use, cost negligible overhead, be production safe, and show everything. Intel has proven it's possible. Feel free to take any claim with a grain of salt, and feel free to wait for an official publication and public launch by Intel on this technology. 1 Based on halving the Arm CEO Rene Haas' estimate of 20-25% quoted in Taking a closer look at AI's supposed energy apocalypse by Kyle Orland of ArsTechnica. Their version looks shallow as it's only the GPU code, so it is missing the CPU context necessary to understand the full picture, and seems based on interposing (launching the app from Nsights) which is the old method. The new method we've created allows for easy, everything, anytime profiling, like you expect from CPU profilers. Theirs does have click-to-source integration, which is quite handy, and I do like the default orientation and colors, thank you! items.headline: Spectral networks, finite webs, and the $T_3$ cubic differential
items.summary: We describe spectral networks for cubic differentials on $\mathbf{P}^1$ with exactly three poles all of order two, following observations of Hollands-Neitzke. To do so, we give a precise definition and establish some basic properties of a class of finite webs (corresponding to BPS states in physics) in the cubic differential setting, including their non-vanishing central charge. Turning to the example, we prove that at rational angles the network is totally degenerate; the number of walls and Stokes regions is explicitly computed and depends on an arithmetic criterion.

items.headline: The semiring of spectral duality skeletons: cancellation, characters and factorization
items.summary: Weighted dual skeletons are the combinatorial core of spectral duality structures. Their isomorphism classes, under Cartesian product and disjoint union, form a semiring graded by the degree. We identify it completely: a class is determined by its degree, a symmetric element of the group semiring N_0[R] and its number of fixed points.

detail.method_architecture: Their isomorphism classes, under Cartesian product and disjoint union, form a semiring graded by the degree. We identify it completely: a class is determined by its degree, a symmetric element of the group semiring N_0[R] and its number of fixed points.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Equivalently, skeletons of a given degree are finite C_2-sets over the C_2-monoid (R,+), these data are their marks, and the semiring is an infinite-monoid analogue of a crossed Burnside semiring. The multiplicative monoid is not cancellative, the only obstruction being that multiplication by a skeleton without fixed points forgets the fixed points; accordingly, the Grothendieck ring has explicit zero divisors. A continuous family of semiring characters, with the degree and the number of fixed points, is a complete invariant, and for commensurable ratios the multiplicative Grothendieck group is described by Pólya's theorem. The main subject is factorization. The reduced monoid is atomic with bounded lengths, but factorization is not unique, the elasticity is infinite, and even the divisor-closed submonoid with one fixed point is not half-factorial. Without fixed points, every reducible skeleton splits off a single orbit, which gives a criterion by centers, exactly when the number of orbits is 8, 16, a prime or twice a prime. Irreducibility is generic in almost every type. Progression skeletons factor according to mixed-radix number systems, with all factorizations of equal length. Finally, orbit counting gives the dimension of the separatrix and the response rank of products.

items.headline: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History
items.summary: Weak-form efficiency implies symmetry restrictions on the Markov chain governing movement across the cryptocurrency capitalisation distribution. We test them on the full listed population: 8,970 assets, 690 weekly cross-sections, 2013 to 2026, with entry, exit and survival observed rather than inferred. Symmetry is rejected in every era, but the asymmetry falls by seventy percent, and what converged is entry-driven compositional churn rather than coins' own valuations.

items.headline: Proportionality in Ranking Compression
items.summary: Motivated by applications in reinforcement learning from human feedback, we consider a setting where a given collection of rankings needs to be compressed into a smaller collection of rankings. This can also be seen as a combination of two fundamental social choice frameworks: ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting. We propose three proportionality notions that capture different types of representation in this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC).

items.headline: The Source of Data Value: Consumer Disclosure, Access Design, and Platform Monetization
items.summary: Digital marketplaces increasingly earn revenue from transaction commissions and seller-facing data services. Sellers may purchase data to increase revenue or avoid competing with an informed rival. We examine how consumer disclosure rights shape these motives and the platform's incentive to provide data.

detail.problem_context: Digital marketplaces increasingly earn revenue from transaction commissions and seller-facing data services.
detail.method_architecture: Sellers may purchase data to increase revenue or avoid competing with an informed rival. We examine how consumer disclosure rights shape these motives and the platform's incentive to provide data.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We develop a game-theoretic model of a commissioned platform, two differentiated sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers. Data generates value through bilateral sales-revenue gains and competition threats arising from asymmetric access. Under mandatory collection, the platform can monetize defensive adoption, even when bilateral personalization reduces seller revenue. Under voluntary disclosure, anonymous purchasing and strictly positive privacy costs make unilateral disclosure unattractive in the baseline. Exclusive access thus yields no usable information, restores sellers' no-data rejection payoffs, and eliminates defensive fees. Profitable provision therefore requires nonnegative bilateral revenue gains. Under full fee extraction, sellers retain their no-data net profits. This revenue alignment does not guarantee welfare gains: additional transactions may benefit consumers, whereas segmentation in an already covered market can raise anonymous prices and reduce welfare. Capping anonymous offers at their no-data benchmark protects individual consumers and limits positive-mass provision to the transaction-creation region. Extensions consider access choice, heterogeneous privacy costs, imperfect identification, and limited contractual credibility. Platforms should evaluate data services based on both bilateral-use and seller-rejection outcomes, and sellers should distinguish revenue-enhancing from defensive investments. Regulators should distinguish equal-access rules from effective consumer control and monitor pricing in anonymous channels.

items.headline: Agentic AI in Automated Markets. Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs).
items.summary: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). We study how heterogeneous agent behavior shapes stress, risk-adjusted performance, liquidity, and volatility in these types of markets. Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower.

detail.problem_context: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs).

Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. Herd-followers produce the most frequent but shortest stress episodes, manipulators the fewest but most persistent, and rational agents the most stable rolling Sharpe ratios despite higher return volatility. SHAP attributions tie these patterns to drawdown and cross-asset signals, short-term volatility and position state, and momentum, respectively. The results motivate behavior-specific regulation rather than uniform limits on volatility or turnover.

items.headline: Anyonic Neural Network Wavefunctions. The macroscopic behavior of a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons has remained unsettled for many decades.
items.summary: The macroscopic behavior of a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons has remained unsettled for many decades. Prior numerical methods employing exact diagonalization in the continuum and on the plane have been limited to small system sizes, at most $N = 4$ anyons. Using the rapidly developing technology of neural network wavefunctions, we develop variational ansatze appropriate for studying continuum models of the Abelian anyon gas.

detail.method_architecture: Prior numerical methods employing exact diagonalization in the continuum and on the plane have been limited to small system sizes, at most $N = 4$ anyons. Using the rapidly developing technology of neural network wavefunctions, we develop variational ansatze appropriate for studying continuum models of the Abelian anyon gas.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: The neural network architecture, which we call "AnyNet", is capable of exactly enforcing the non-analytic short-distance behavior induced by the anyonic statistics. We demonstrate excellent agreement with exact diagonalization for $N=4$ anyons, obtain accurate results up to $N = 16$ for intermediate statistics, and study up to $N=20$ for almost-fermionic anyons, matching perturbative results within a 0.4% discrepancy. We use this methodology to study anyons in a harmonic trap, and anyonic atoms as a model for anyon binding to impurities. We study the structure of anyonic wavefunctions as the statistics parameter is varied. We focus on the single-particle density, the pair density, the angular momentum, and the scaling of the wavefunction as multiple anyons coalesce. This work opens doors to understanding the macroscopic behavior of anyons, for which rich phases have been predicted theoretically.

items.headline: Orbital Angular Momentum Currents and Textures in a Multiorbital Double Helix

items.headline: Engineering nonrelativistic spin splitting in semiconductors by altermagnetic proximity
items.summary: Altermagnets combine vanishing net magnetization with momentum-dependent, nonrelativistic spin splitting, offering functionalities attractive for spintronics and quantum devices. Their practical use, however, is constrained by the limited availability of materials that simultaneously possess the required altermagnetic symmetry, semiconducting electronic structure, and weak spin-orbit coupling. Here we show that these requirements can instead be separated between constituent materials through proximity engineering.

items.headline: Temperature and Thickness Dependent Spin Current Transmission through Epitaxial Antiferromagnetic α-Fe2O3
items.summary: Antiferromagnetic insulator α-Fe2O3 is a potential medium for coherent motion of spin waves over relatively large distances, allowing non-dissipative transfer of information between circuit elements. However, the structural defects and temperature dependent spin reorientations in this oxide impact the propagation. Understanding how the magnetic state of an antiferromagnetic insulator affects spin-current transmission is therefore important for elucidating the mechanisms governing spin transport.

items.headline: Limits from nonlinear loss of spin-orbit-torque control of magnon transport
items.summary: Controlling magnon currents is central to the development of magnonic devices, which exploit spin excitations for information transport without charge flow. Here, we use the spin-orbit torque (SOT) from a Pt gate to control the effective magnon damping in three-terminal devices fabricated from low-damping lithium aluminum ferrite (LAFO) thin films and identify the nonlinear damping that ultimately limits the gate response. With increasing gate current, the nonlocal magnon signal initially increases, but saturates and subsequently decreases above a critical gate current density.

items.headline: Holographic two-point functions across a PT symmetry-breaking transition
items.summary: In parity-time (PT)-symmetric non-Hermitian systems, an exceptional point, where eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, typically separates a real spectrum from complex-conjugate eigenvalues. In logarithmic conformal field theories (LCFTs), such an exceptional point appears in the spectrum of scaling dimensions. Holographic models of LCFTs, such as the dipole model, are built exactly at this point.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Here, we deform the holographic dipole model so that its two coalescing scaling dimensions split into either two real ones or a complex-conjugate pair. We obtain the renormalized two-point functions in closed form. They change continuously from a linear combination of two power laws, through the logarithmic form of the LCFT at the exceptional point, to log-periodic oscillations. For any pair of scalar primary operators with real mixing under dilatations, the conformal Ward identities fix this form up to two normalization constants, which the holographic dictionary determines. In PT-symmetric theories with such a dilatation operator, real and complex-conjugate scaling dimensions correspond to the PT-unbroken and PT-broken phases. In the BTZ black hole at finite temperature, the difference between the quasinormal frequencies associated with the two scaling dimensions changes from purely imaginary to purely real across the real-to-complex spectral transition. Correspondingly, the linear response changes from overdamped to underdamped, with critical damping at the exceptional point.

items.headline: Renormalization Group Domain Walls from Phantom Symmetries. We develop a systematic construction of renormalization group (RG) domain walls between two-dimensional rational conformal field theories.
items.summary: We develop a systematic construction of renormalization group (RG) domain walls between two-dimensional rational conformal field theories. The construction of RG walls then reduces to identifying suitable automorphism-twisted Cardy states in the auxiliary theory.

items.headline: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
items.summary: Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies.

items.summary: Classical execution models assume linear impact, diffusive prices, and an exogenous horizon. We study execution under concave power-law impact and Hurst-scaled price fluctuations, and make two contributions. First, we choose the execution horizon by maximizing the Sharpe ratio of the trade's realized P&L.

detail.method_architecture: We study execution under concave power-law impact and Hurst-scaled price fluctuations, and make two contributions. First, we choose the execution horizon by maximizing the Sharpe ratio of the trade's realized P&L.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Price moves during the execution window are part of that P&L, so executing more slowly reduces its variance, and because impact is concave it can also lower cost per share. Urgency comes only from alpha realized while the order is being worked. The problem is governed by the signs of two quantities: (i) the duration elasticity of impact $a$, which under a structural prior equals the impact-persistence gap $β- H$ and can take either sign; and (ii) the net urgency $ν$, the rate of alpha realization net of exposure relief. When $ν$ keeps its sign over the window, an interior optimum exists, to leading order in $T/t_f$, only when both are positive; otherwise the order should be worked at the fastest or slowest admissible pace. In the interior regime the first-order condition involves no impact coefficient, order size or volume, and the objective is flat: for a large-cap example, the window within 1% of maximal Sharpe spans more than an order of magnitude. Second, given the window, we derive the schedule shape by convex programming under an envelope cost. For any increasing per-share cost of delay $w(t)$, the KKT solution is $φ\propto (λ- w(t))_+^{1/β}$. For a Hurst-scaled envelope $w \propto t^H$, the normalized schedule depends only on $(β, H)$, has a closed form via the incomplete beta function, is front-loaded, and tapers smoothly to zero, saving 10-17% of envelope cost relative to a constant-rate (TWAP) schedule of equal duration. Whether it uses the whole window depends on a single dimensionless robustness level, for which we give a calibration.

items.headline: Recursive Operator Localization and Spectral Gap Descent via the Geometry of Local Spectral Expansion
items.summary: We introduce Recursive Operator Localization (ROL), a framework for constructing hierarchies of local energy problems linked by linear maps between Hilbert spaces. To address spectral-gap problems, including those arising in quantum systems, we study a realization of ROL by nested subspaces indexed by a weighted simplicial complex. Using spectral gaps of auxiliary classical random walks on links, we propagate geometric estimates upward and use them to turn local spectral gaps at the bottom of the hierarchy into a spectral-gap bound for the global operator.

The framework also offers a route toward quantum Gibbs sampling, with applications requiring model-specific geometric estimates and energy comparisons.

items.summary: Threshold implementations (TIs) are now an established class of side-channel countermeasures. Their underlying idea is simple and compelling: under mild, practical assumptions, they provide protection against glitches and allow composability. Yet our understanding of one-stage TIs with a minimal number of shares remains limited, both for cryptographically relevant families—particularly power functions—and for concrete small functions.

items.headline: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems
items.summary: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable.

detail.problem_context: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee.
detail.method_architecture: The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized. Polkadot enforces conservative update rates, effectively disabling fee adaptivity and reverting the market to inefficient first-price auctions. Cosmos adopts aggressive update rates without formal guarantees. To fill this gap, we propose a control-theoretic framework that formalizes multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback. We identify delay-amplified over-correction as the structural root of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling erodes stability relative to monolithic blockchains, reducing the safe parameter space for base fee update rates by up to 84.8%. Moreover, instability propagates across chains, contaminating the otherwise stable peer chains. At Ethereum's update rate, which leaves a monolithic chain stable, the multi-chain system exhibits extreme load oscillation between full and near-empty blocks, with over half of all blocks at full capacity. Mainstream Cosmos chains already exceed their safe bounds under their default configurations, and the resulting load oscillation raises their block failure rate by an order of magnitude. Guided by this mechanism, we design a lightweight protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction and stabilizes dynamics in multi-chain environments.

items.headline: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
items.summary: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-Lévy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $α$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. items.headline: How Much Screening Buys a Second? Speed, Selection, and the Maker's Spread
items.summary: We study the spread a liquidity provider needs to break even against counterparties that can exploit a stale quote, and we place two defenses on a single scale: repricing sooner and screening informed flow. A break-even condition pins down the exact screening rate at which a slower maker matches a faster unscreened venue: the selection that buys back the extra staleness. The result requires only an integrable price innovation and therefore holds under jumps, atoms and infinite variance.

detail.findings_tradeoffs:
We take the model to four USDC-WETH pools benchmarked against Binance ETH-USDT from June to August 2026. TLDR The one-second benchmark innovation is sharply non-Gaussian: 73% of seconds show no price change, and the excess kurtosis is 154; Cutting cadence from twelve seconds to one sheds 84.5% of the expected shock, so a twelve-second maker must screen at least 84.5% of informed flow to match a one-second venue, far above the 71.1% that a Gaussian model implies; The conclusion does not depend on pinning toxicity down: over the informed shares admitted by the tightest netting bound, the threshold stays between 84.5% and 85.2%. Matching one-second execution from a twelve-second slot is worth screening out roughly six in seven informed orders; In trending markets, the stale pool is picked off at execution: with-trend fills obtain an effective spread 11.1 bps lower than against-trend fills, with the same sign in all four pools; Missed proposer slots show the discrepancy a stale pool must absorb growing with elapsed staleness at an elasticity of 0.45, close to the diffusion rate of one-half; Predictable drift is a centering problem: it widens a spot-centered quote, but its cost vanishes once the quote is recentered on the expected reference. 1. Why does staleness matter for liquidity providers? An LP who posts a firm two-sided quote has written an option on the asset. Traders who know where the price is heading exercise it against the maker, while everyone else trades by chance. The maker recovers what the informed take from the spread it charges the rest. The competitive spread is the width at which the two balance: losses to better-informed counterparties are repaid by earnings from everyone else. Automated market makers, or AMMs, make this option unusually stark. A constant-function pool quotes a deterministic price off its reserves and refreshes only when someone trades against it. Between trades, the quote is stale, and on a chain that settles in discrete blocks, it can stay stale for the whole block, roughly twelve seconds on the network we study. With no last look and no way to pull a posted quote, an arbitrageur watching a faster venue picks the pool off the moment the external price clears fees. A maker has two defenses: shorten the time its quote is exposed, or screen the flow and decline the orders most likely to be informed. Which defense is available depends on the venue. A permissionless pool must fill every order that clears its invariant, so its only lever is exposure; a proprietary or curated maker can do both. Our question is how much a second of reduced staleness is worth against a unit of screening, and when one substitutes for the other. Three following features organize the paper: The threshold is scale-free. Under a driftless diffusion it depends only on the ratio of the two horizons and the informed share 	heta , not on volatility, fee, or trade size. Tail shape matters. The threshold’s response to toxicity is governed by the expected loss on an executed informed order, so a fat-tailed innovation and a Gaussian one of equal variance imply very different spreads and screening thresholds: the shape of the tail, not just its width, is what the maker prices. Drift is a centering problem. A predictable price component tilts which side gets picked off and widens a quote held at the current reference, but a maker that centers its quote on the expected reference recovers the driftless spread. 2. Each swap is timed at its block’s slot time, read from the block header, and after removing dust swaps, the sample holds 1,725,539 swaps. The batch-netting statistic uses the full Binance trade tape of 260 million trades. Both ratios are reported in basis points throughout. The local drift \hat{\mu}_t is the trailing sixty-second benchmark return, and a second is trending when |\hat{\mu}_t| > 10 bps; by this cut, 88.9% of seconds are range-bound and 11.1% trending, and 318,822 of the swaps fall in trending seconds. Feature engineering For the v3 pools, we read the direction and the price from the signed amounts: the taker direction is the sign of the pool’s signed USDC amount, and the executed price is the ratio of the traded amounts. Wherever consecutive swap records chain, this direction agrees with the post-swap price path on 99.88–100% of fills. The pool-minus-benchmark deviation is then basis-adjusted by subtracting its own three-hundred-second rolling median, which absorbs the slow USDC/USDT basis. Against the raw ETH-USDT mid, the median effective spread is 7.7 to 29.7 bps across pools, and after the adjustment it is 1.0 to 10.2 bps. Panel B is a diagnostic of the toxicity proxy we ultimately discard: the share of trades with a positive five-second markout sits at 0.34–0.40 in every pool, as expected of a statistic driven by the symmetric innovation rather than by the informed share. The persistent pool-benchmark gap is a slow stablecoin basis, typically -5 to -10 bps, that drifts over weeks, not intra-slot staleness. The reference and identification The Binance quoted spread is one tick wide almost always, with a median of 0.0538 bps. This is the empirical floor, i.e., the price of liquidity under no cadence constraint whatsoever, and it is the number every model spread below should be read against. Re-pricing every pool against the last trade instead of the mid leaves the basis-adjusted effective spread essentially unchanged. Every causal statement rests on one assumption: at the one-second to one-minute horizon, the benchmark mid, its increments, and the drift are predetermined with respect to any single pool’s idiosyncratic order flow. Binance turns over orders of magnitude more volume than the four pools and leads price discovery, so the pools are price-takers that re-converge to the benchmark through arbitrage. A slot-level lead-lag regression confirms this ordering directly: the pool absorbs 96% of a Binance move within a minute and does not lead it. 3. The pooled pick-off gap, i.e., the difference in effective spread between with-trend and against-trend fills in the trending regime, equals -11.1 bps with pool fixed effects (hour-clustered standard error 0.41, t = -27.3 ; shift test p < 0.002 ). With-trend fills execute at -1.71 bps, better than the benchmark mid, while against-trend fills pay 6.97 bps. The gap has the predicted sign and is significant in all four pools: -7.6 bps in the v3 1 bp pool, -11.3 bps in the v3 5 bps pool, -69.4 bps in the v3 30 bps pool, and -60.9 bps in the v2 pool. In the two thirty-basis-point pools it is about twice the fee, because with-trend flow there trades when the stale price covers the fee, while against-trend flow pays the fee in full. With-trend takers also arrive after a larger benchmark move: over the twelve seconds before the block, the benchmark moves 4.85 bps in the trend’s direction before with-trend fills and 2.77 bps before against-trend fills. Once the block lands, the benchmark does not move further in the taker’s favor: the five-second markout gap is -0.06 bps and not significant, so the stale-quote loss is realized at execution rather than after it. The screening threshold The model’s central comparison has a direct empirical counterpart: the rate at which a twelve-second maker must screen to match a one-second venue. In the low-toxicity limit, evaluated on the empirical innovation, it equals 1 - 0.292/1.880 \approx 84.5\% , 13.3 percentage points above the driftless Gaussian benchmark of 1 - 1/\sqrt{12} \approx 71.1\% , because \kappa falls faster with cadence than \sqrt{h} would predict. Positive serial dependence at the one-second horizon accounts for about 3 points of the gap, and the shape of the one-second innovation for the remaining 10: most seconds are calm and a minority carry large moves, which aggregation to twelve seconds averages out. Across alternative references (the BBA mid, the microprice, a trade-implied mid, and the last trade), it ranges from 84.0% to 85.1%. Solving the exact break-even at positive toxicity raises both curves and, because the empirical curve is the flatter of the two, they nearly meet at high toxicity: at 	heta = 0.706 the empirical threshold is 87.8% against the Gaussian 86.4%. Over the informed shares admitted by the tightest netting bound, the empirical threshold stays between 84.5% and 85.2%, and up to 	heta = 0.9 between 84.5% and 90.9%, so the conclusion does not depend on pinning toxicity down. Screening would have to be extraordinarily effective, rejecting on the order of 85% of informed opportunities, for a block-cadence maker to match one-second execution on this pair. The equal-cadence premium quantifies the converse: a one-second maker that screens even a quarter of informed flow already prices 0.084 bps inside an unscreened one-second venue, whose half-spread is 0.454 bps, rising to 0.302 bps at three-quarters screening. Robustness Moving the drift-sign series circularly by at least an hour preserves its persistence and the timing of every fill while breaking its alignment with the fills; over 500 such shifts, no draw exceeds 1.1 bps in absolute value against the observed -11.1 bps. On a chronological holdout, the benchmark return in the direction of the trailing drift averages only +0.064 bps over the next twelve seconds: predictable drift is small in this sample, so the pick-off documented above reflects staleness rather than drift, and a recentered quote would gain little over a spot-centered one. The calm-window placebo is passed: outside trends the markout gap is accounted for by the benchmark’s own continuation. 5. What this means for liquidity providers 1. Speed is the cheap defense. Cutting cadence from twelve seconds to one sheds 84.5% of the expected shock and cuts the break-even half-spread by 73% to 85% at a fixed informed share. 2. Screening alone rarely substitutes for speed. Matching one-second execution from a twelve-second slot is worth screening out roughly six in seven informed orders, and more at higher toxicity. 3. At equal speed, screening still pays. Screening narrows the spread by strictly less than the screening rate times the unscreened spread, because the narrower spread makes additional informed opportunities profitable, but a quarter of informed flow screened already prices 0.084 bps inside an unscreened venue. 4. Do not price with Gaussian rules of thumb. The tail shape, not just its width, is what the maker prices; the volatility-anchored rule overstates the spread by up to 7 	imes , and the Gaussian understates the screening threshold by 13 points. 5. Recenter rather than widen. Predictable drift is a centering problem rather than a spread problem: a maker that centers its quote on the expected terminal reference removes the drift premium entirely. 6. Limitations Toxicity is not point-identified. The batch-netting residual is an upper bound whose excess over a run-preserving null is indistinguishable from zero, so we report the threshold across informed shares up to that bound, over which it moves by less than one percentage point. The model holds potential flow fixed and resets each quote to the reference, which abstracts both from the change in counterparty composition that faster repricing can induce and from the fee-determined no-arbitrage band of an AMM. Screening is costless and independent of opportunity size, whereas a classifier that preferentially rejects the most profitable informed orders would call for a loss-weighted threshold. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic

We have an accompanied repo for scheme 3 which is the best first step to PQ SAP upgrade Recalling ML-KEM We adopt FIPS 203 for ML-KEM Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard , published 13 August 2024. A KEM (Key-Encapsulation Mechanism) consists of three algorithms and a collection of parameter sets. The three algorithms are: A probabilistic key generation algorithm denoted by KeyGen A probabilistic “encapsulation” algorithm denoted by Encaps A deterministic “decapsulation” algorithm denoted by Decaps Alice : Bob : +------------------+ : | KeyGen | : +------------------+ : | | : | +-----------------:--------------------+ v : v +------------------+ : +------------------+ | decapsulation key| : | encapsulation key| +------------------+ : +------------------+ | : | v : v +------------------+ +------:-----+ +------------------+ | Decaps |<---| ciphertext |<----| Encaps | +------------------+ +------:-----+ +------------------+ | : | v : v +------------------+ : +------------------+ | Alice's copy of | : | Bob's copy of | | the shared secret| : | the shared secret| +------------------+ : +------------------+ : r' : r A KEM is used to establish a shared secret between two parties Alice and Bob as described above. This is what we call indistinguishability of keys (IK-CCA, a.k.a ANO-CCA), which turns out to be important for SAP. Does ML-KEM offer ANO-CCA? Intuitively and fortunately, yes. There is a dedicated analysis of Post-Quantum Anonymity of Kyber in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). As specified, the FIPS 203 transform matches the intermediate transform in Figure 6 of the analysis: it returns the first half of G on valid encapsulations and uses a separate ciphertext-dependent rejection key on invalid ciphertexts. H(r')[0] after recovering r' (instead of another EC scalar multiplication, and EC addition and a hash, albeit this is of a different proportion w.r.t schemeId-1), WITH SOME ANONYMITY RISK (see below). ERC5564Announcer does not need to be modified except for perhaps a naming change, to emit respective events to announce when something is sent to a stealth address ( Announcement(uint256 indexed schemeId, address indexed stealthAddress, address indexed caller, bytes mlKEMciphertext, bytes metadata) ). However, with ML-KEM-768, the mlKEMciphertext is 1088 bytes. ERC6538Registry which centralizes the registration and retrieval of public stealth meta addresses can keep current form ( mapping(address registrant => mapping(uint256 schemeId => bytes)) ). However, with ML-KEM-768, the encapsulation key size is 1184 bytes, the bytes part will be increased by 1151 bytes. The naive ViewTag vs CRQC Recalling that P = K + hG = (k+h)G h^* = h[0] a CRQC that knows the derived public key P can: recover p=\log_G(P) ; recover k_i=\log_G(K_i) for each candidate public spending key K_i in the registry; compute h_i=(p-k_i)\bmod n and test whether h_i[0]=h^* . The correct recipient passes while an independently generated wrong candidate passes with probability approximately 1/256 . This gives a recipient-linkage filter without breaking ML-KEM. The attack requires P , which becomes recoverable from an ordinary ECDSA spend. We can prevent this direct test by deriving the tweak and view tag independently from the shared secret: h=H(DS1 \parallel r) h^*=H(DS2 \parallel r)[0] The sender knows r from encapsulation, and the receiver or scanner obtains it through decapsulation. Recovering h through quantum discrete logarithms does not directly reveal the independently derived tag. Thus, the tag’s privacy depends on the protected shared secret r , without requiring the sender to know dk . This attack is applicable to all ECDSA-based SAPs attempting to upgrade to PQ anonymity via ML-KEM (2-5 in this post).
